newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's new VP urges unity against rebels.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's new VP urges unity against rebels.

text.p: Colombia's new vice president was sworn into office on Tuesday and immediately urged his divided countrymen to unite against the left-wing insurgents whom he said were threatening to cause a "national catastrophe."
"We have to realise that a country at war can be saved not by malice but solidarity," Carlos Lemos Simmonds said in a speech at the ornate presidential palace after his swearing-in ceremony.
"If the enemies of Colombia have joined together to destroy us we can't remain divided and confronting one another without necessarily becoming accomplices in the national catastrophe," he said.
"Guerrillas who are mobilising toward the centres of power ... can only be stopped by the entire country, united if only for that one vital purpose which cannot be postponed," he said.
Lemos, 63, Colombia's ambassador to Britain and a widely respected former cabinet minister, was sworn in to replace Humberto de la Calle, who resigned as vice president last month.

De la Calle cited the prolonged political crisis stemming from President Ernesto Samper's alleged links to drug lords as his reason for stepping down. He said the government had lost all credibility, was wallowing in corruption, and appeared powerless in the face of guerrillas -- who launched their most dramatic offensive in more than three decades of war in late August.

Lemos, who has a reputation as a rightist with a leaning toward authoritarian-style rule, did not deny that Colombia has been deeply divided by the crisis that erupted more than a year ago over charges that Samper used drug money to finance his bid for the presidency.

But given the seriousness of the guerrilla offensive, he said it was time for Colombians to end their "self-destructive in-fighting" and rally around the government and military in their time of need.

Calling counterinsurgency efforts "the great national objective," he added that all Colombians except sworn enemies of peace could surely agree on the desirability of being able "to walk through the streets and fields of Colombia without fearing the loss of liberty and life."

Samper also called for popular support of the military in his address to the swearing-in ceremony, and dismissed critics of the army's poor human rights record by asking "what liberties and what human rights are valid amid anarchy and violence?"

The embattled president reiterated his call for passage of legislation that would give the executive branch sweeping powers to declare virtual military rule in areas of the country torn by guerrilla activity.

And while he conceded that Colombia's two largest guerrilla groups, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia and National Liberation Army, had inflicted widepsread damage across the country in the past month, he insisted that the national security situation was now under control.

In a parting shot at the rebels -- whom diplomats and Western military experts say have seized the initiative and humiliated the army repeatedly in recent weeks -- Samper said they were nothing but bandits, kidnappers and drug traffickers whose actions were devoid of the "social content" motivating their counterparts in the jungles and mountains of southern Mexico.
